newsitem.title: UK: Tobacco's addictive nature well known, experts say.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco's addictive nature well known, experts say.

text.p: Doctors, psychologists and anti-smoking campaigners say they have had proof for years that smoking not only causes cancer and heart disease, but is as addictive as heroin or cocaine.
Even hard-core smokers admit they know smoking is dangerous, and many confess they are addicted. So how has the tobacco industry managed to deny it for so long?
"I think it just shows the power of their lawyers," said Amanda Sandford of anti-smoking campaign group ASH.
"It is incredible that they have been able to get away with it for so long."
On Thursday U.S. tobacco company Liggett Group made the astonishing move of admitting that smoking damages health and is addictive.

"At last a tobacco company has acknowledged publicly what the rest of the world has acknowledged for at least 25 years," said Dr Martin Jarvis, an addiction expert for the Imperial Cancer Research Fund.
Experts say about three million people die each year from smoking-related illness in developed countries, representing 20 percent of all deaths.
"Every 10 seconds, another person dies as a result of tobacco use," the World Health Organisation says.
Eight different types of cancer, from lung cancer to leukaemia, are linked with smoking and smoking is the single biggest risk factor for heart disease.
Even the tobacco industry has mostly given up on this fight, arguing that smoking is a matter of choice -- something else bitterly denied by health campaigners.
"The evidence that it is powerfully addictive is absolutely overwhelming," Jarvis said in an interview.

Of more than 61,000 people surveyed by the U.S. Centres for Disease Control, 79.6 percent of daily cigarette smokers said they could not cut down. Only 66 percent of daily cocaine users said they could not.

A survey last year by British cancer charities and the British Medical Association found that one in 12 teenage smokers lit up within five minutes of waking and said this indicated they became addicted very quickly.
"It's a kind of stimulant drug, a bit like amphetamine. One of the thoughts about why cigarettes are so addictive is the route of administration," Jarvis said.
"When you inhale it in smoke you are getting the drug hitting the brain within seven to 10 seconds, which is actually faster than if you injected it," he said.
"It is also cleared from the body very rapidly so you have to keep getting yourself a hit to keep levels up."
Jarvis said scientists were beginning to understand the effects of nicotine on the brain. It seems to literally excite brain cells.

In July neuroscientists at Italy's University of Cagliari found that nicotine helped increase the transmission of dopamine, an important neurotransmitter, or chemical that carries messages between brain cells.

Researchers at Brookhaven National Laboratory in Upton, New York found last year that smokers had less of an enzyme called monoamine oxidase (MAO), which breaks down dopamine, than ex-smokers or people who do not smoke. This would mean more dopamine was available to their brains. Drugs such as cocaine and heroin have a similar effect.
Other research has shown that nicotine locks on to areas in the brain that release acetylcholine, another neurotransmitter that sets off electrical impulses in nerve and muscle cells.
Yet others have found it causes nerve cells to send out a larger-than-normal amount of glutamate, an excitory transmittor which, as the name implies, excites or stimulates cells.
